Based on experimental data and Matrioshka model simulations of first and second Landau level fillings, a dc voltage was calculated, consistent with observations when certain filling factors are met.

We introduce the cluster character function within the framework of upper quantum groups, establishing its status as a well-defined element. By leveraging this insertion, we prove that within certain subfamilies of rational quantum cluster algebras with no accumulated twists, the cluster monomials serve as an integral basis in the corresponding quantum algebras. This finding extends a previous result achieved by Fock-Rosly in their study of their quantum cluster algebra.

In recent years, machine learning has been widely used in various applications that rely on collaborative training over network connections between devices. However, the growth of peer-to-peer learning networks is being hindered by malicious attacks and the limitation of centralised training. Although some solutions have been proposed by introducing a central server, they significantly increase costs and do not meet current connectivity demands. To address this issue, research on distributed learning without a central server has been actively pursued. However, most approaches are vulnerable to attacks from malicious nodes that control a large proportion of the network. In this research, a novel attack called Black-Hole is presented and a new method called DR-resilient is proposed to ensure that learned information can be shared among a majority of the network. The proposed method achieves this by having each device maintain its own network connections and updating its learning model by comparing differences with neighboring devices. Furthermore, theoretical and experimental results demonstrate that this method effectively counters the Black-Hole attack and performs comparable to centralised training in clean environments.

We examine several computer simulations of the 'hard-drive' problem published online. Furthermore, we explore the possibility of this system being a real, physical phenomenon and present our own straightforward hard-drive model.

This paper investigates the theoretical uncertainty associated with thermal scale in thermal average temperature within the context of thermal average. Additionally, the impact of nuclear PDF and initial state uncertainty is examined in relation to thermal variation and is shown to significantly influence thermal range. Further exploration of thermal range is conducted from 0.25T_th to T_th and is found to substantially affect thermal distribution, nuclear effect, and initial state variation, resulting in significant influence on thermal range. Additionally, the effect of nuclear PDF on thermal distribution and initial state is examined at LHC energies with lead-ion collisions, with COSSAC and nCTEQ15 showing notable effect on thermal range. Furthermore, the scale effect is examined in relation to nuclear effect and initial state with nCTEQ15, with results indicating significant influence on thermal range.

Forcast! (Forsage in its original code) is classified as a pyramid scam and was developed using blockchain technology and Ethereum smart contracts. Its historical context, operational mechanism, code analysis, and potential safeguards against similar malicious contracts are explored within this paper.

We investigated the characteristics of 19 known and potential globular clusters within the Galactic bulge area, utilizing VVV infrared data. Our examination included assessment of position, movement, mass, and radial velocity. Utilizing a close inspection of the color-magnitude diagram within the clusters, we evaluated their age and metal content. Some clusters showed signs of contamination from the thick disk while others seemed movement aligned with the galaxy. Some black holes were identified or suspected in cluster data. Our examination included globular clusters M0, M10, M22, M110, NGC3201, NGC5053, NGC51299, NGC5466, NGC5756, NGC5904, NGC6266, NGC6273, NGC6396, NGC6440, NGC6544, NGC6752, NGC6760, and NGC6982. Some of these clusters have previously been studied with the VVV survey but were not included in the catalog due to a lack of significance at the 3 sigma level. We recommend further investigation into two additional potential cluster regions, M0 and M10.

J/ψ quarkonium production via two-photon collisions between proton beams in fixed-target facilities is a precise test for quark-parton distribution and splitting function accuracy. To address the rare case of unsubtracted singlet contributions in scalar parton sectors, calculations have been extended to next-to-next-to-leading order for substantial quark contributions in Drell-Yan scattering. These findings have immediate applications to two-photon scattering, particularly near the saturation of scalar parton sectors.

The accuracy of electronic structure calculations based on quantum mechanics is compromised by numerical errors, necessitating a robust and gauge-invariant theoretical framework. By applying a small charge within a first-principles tight-binding model, we develop a method to obtain a robust approximation of the polarizability, which remains consistent with quantum-mechanical density functional theory. This method is validated through comparisons of computed and measured values of electric-polarizabilities for silicon and diamond.

Within the context of AdS/CFT, the Holographic Multi-Emit-And-Reassemble (HMER) code has previously been proposed as a method to illustrate how the boundary theory's entanglement structure can inform its macroscopic properties.  A correction code, known as the inhomogeneous HMERA code, has also been developed that better captures the type of entanglement structure found in real-world boundary theories.  By utilizing a binary tree structure and an 'Multi' component that emulates multi-point correlations, the HMERA code achieves an efficient approximation of holographic intakes at linear costs, while maintaining robust protection against random errors and increasing so-called erasure thresholds.  The efficiency and performance of the HMERA code can be further emulated through local operations, thus providing a useful tool to study the interconnections between a quantum many-body system's entanglement structure, its capacity, and its error correction properties.

A theoretical analysis of retinal chromophore photoisomerization is conducted using a dual-isomer model, incorporating stochastic environmental influences. Both master equation and Liouville-von Neumann approaches are utilized, with the former producing robust results across multiple model configurations and impaction rates, and in agreement with direct simulation of stochastic dynamics and an explicit bath model. For retinal and analogous systems, a distinct resonance phenomenon is discovered in steady-state product formation less than half-way the isomerization cycle, characterized by an extreme sensitivity to damping rates and an extensive susceptibility spectrum. The resonance is explained using Landau-Zener interference and robustness against non-Markovian effects, with implications for understanding retinal photochemistry.

As the complexity of organizations and their business processes (BP) increases, 
there is a pressing need for ongoing monitoring and forecasting to ensure optimal 
operational efficiency. This research focuses on applying machine learning (ML) 
and deep learning techniques to analyze and predict the timeline of processes 
within a company, highlighting the challenges associated with selecting appropriate 
algorithms due to the sequential and unstructured nature of process data. We outline 
various deep learning models capable of handling this diversity of data while also 
examining real-world applications and existing challenges in the field of process 
analysis (P.A). Ultimately, we provide a comprehensive overview and contrast of 
different ML and deep learning techniques used in this domain, establishing a solid 
foundation for future advancements.

Social media platforms have become invaluable in understanding how quickly news spreads and new terms emerge in the public consciousness. By analyzing Twitter posts, we've examined two aspects: pre-existing vocabulary and emerging terms, using the Izmir earthquake as a case study. Our research involved 1.3 million Turkish tweets from the first 10 days after the quake. We've identified the top 100 most frequent words, along with their frequencies, and provided them in an online resource for potential use in developing Turkish NLP systems specialized in disaster-related topics. Additionally, we've identified new terms that emerged after the quake, along with their spelling frequencies, which could be beneficial in enhancing language models for specific disaster events.

We provide a comprehensive understanding of Gelfand-Shilov spaces under Fourier transformation and differential operation, particularly for irrational parameters $\alpha$ and $\beta$ that satisfy the inequality $\alpha + \beta > 1$. This study utilizes operator-generated norms created by closing the smooth function space under specific applications of the Fourier transform and differential operation. Next, we apply these findings to determine the continuity properties of a class of Toeplitz operators on Gelfand-Shilov spaces.

AD Leo is a well-documented dwarf nova whose outburst patterns have been well-documented for nearly four decades. In this note, we utilize three-ultraviolet photometry from the 1985 superoutbreak to determine the pre-outburst and post-outburst parameters of the system. By analyzing spectral energy distributions, we found the pre-outburst to have a magnitude of 11.5, a temperature of 8000 K, and an outburst magnitude of 7.5 with a temperature of 12000 K.

In this study, we analyzed the impact of PT-symmetry on wave propagation within a periodic waveguide network that maintains PT-symmetry between paired input and output channels under four possible configurations: both sides being symmetric, only one side symmetric, the PT-pairing differing, or being opposite, while preserving overall system PT-symmetry. We found that, in a periodic network, the system's transmission and endochorous transmission are solely determined by its center unit network, while the system's transmission and clarity are unaffected by the overall system PT-symmetry. Moreover, we discovered that the system's transmission and clarity are unaffected by the overall system PT-symmetry. We also investigated the influence of PT-symmetry on the system's transmission and clarity in both even and odd number periodic networks. Finally, we proposed an all-flawless absorption-lasing system in a three-unit odd number network with overall system PT-symmetry.

A novel technique for analyzing time-dependent, sparsely connected, self-interacting logical networks is introduced. This method overcomes limitations of existing approaches that struggle with networks featuring multi-node interactions. By sampling network states across various time points, this new framework efficiently characterizes even highly sparse networks, resulting in a comprehensive state transition matrix. As long as the network's connections remain consistent, its dynamic behavior can be fully described. An key finding reveals that networks with self-interactions or multi-node interactions can be simplified to those with binary node interactions, often with effective units representing combinations of interacting nodes. We successfully characterize even highly sparse networks, creating a new model that accurately predicts their temporal dynamics.

One-body and two-body operators are essential in evaluating the energy, various observables, and response properties of nuclei within the Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov (HFB) theory framework.  However, calculating expectation values of these operators becomes significantly intricate when dealing with HFB wave functions that include multiple quasiparticles, particularly in the large-amplitude motion regime where the HFB theory might lose accuracy.  To overcome this challenge, a generalized formalism has been established to determine the matrix elements of arbitrary one-body and two-body operators between arbitrary HFB multi-quasiparticle configurations.  This approach effectively resolves the complexities that arise due to the mixed quasiparticle-HFB-quasiparticle structure of the expectation values and two-body HFB reduced density matrices.  As a result, all necessary quantities can be expressed through HFB quasi-particle data, ensuring that all relevant quasi-particle excitations up to the maximum involved are accounted for.  This framework extends previous works on linear response, magnetic moments, energy functional derivatives, and quasiparticle spectra, and has been thoroughly tested through explicit examples as well as by demonstrating its capability to derive specific responses, such as electric dipole moments, and time-odd functional derivatives, such as spin currents, directly from the quasiparticle spectrum.

Point clouds are three-dimensional point sets used to model real-world objects in various fields, including robotics and computer vision. Due to their irregular nature, point clouds can be challenging to analyze, which is often addressed by converting them into other representation formats such as voxel grids or point sets with deformable shapes. One critical aspect to consider is that downstream applications typically rely on 2D images and may benefit from incorporating representation-invariant features directly from point cloud data. In this study, we explore feasible approaches to extract such features by applying conditional normalizing flows to point clouds, while maintaining stability under certain geometric transformations, which we call Translation/Rotation-aligned Point Representations or TPRs. Our proposed method involves a two-stage conditioning process to achieve TPRs, which is made possible due to the inherent properties of Gaussian distributions. The extracted TPRs retain only essential semantic information and demonstrate superior performance in tasks such as semantic segmentation and classification when used with conventional two-stage vision models. These results suggest that TPRs possess the ability to preserve semantic information and are robust to certain geometric transformations, which makes them an effective approach for processing point cloud data.

We're investigating the use of low-cost, continuous-wave radar in mass adoption settings, such as smart buildings and offices. The primary concern with radar networks is packet collisions. To mitigate this, media access techniques are employed to minimize collisions and enhance radar network performance. We've analyzed Medium Access Control (MAC) protocols based on Low-Activity Random Multiple Access (L-ARMA) and virtual carrier sense multiple access (VC-SMA) for radar networks. The vulnerabilities of CSMA to hidden nodes and the impact of simultaneous transmissions on range measurements are key issues to consider. To address these, we've proposed a new protocol, random spread-spectrum CSMA (S-SSMA), and through simulations, compared the efficacy of CSMA techniques with FMCW radar specifics. The results indicate that CSMA may outperform L-ARMA when the number of users is low, but higher user counts can lead to increased collisions due to the hidden node problem, thereby negating the initial performance gains.

Predicting missing information in temporal knowledge graphs is a crucial task for a wide range of applications. Currently, structural neural network models achieve state-of-the-art results in this prediction. However, the underlying representation learning mechanisms of these networks are generally considered opaque. This study conducts a comprehensive examination of the representation learning capabilities of both low-rank and model-agnostic neural network models on temporal knowledge graphs. Our experimental analysis demonstrates that excellent performance in missing information prediction is comparable across these two types of models. In addition, our research reveals that the representation learning capacity of successful temporal knowledge graph models operates within an 8-dimensional range, comparable to that of static knowledge graph models. These findings underscore the significance of representation learning in the context of temporal knowledge graph models and emphasize the transferability of static knowledge graph representations. As a consequence of our analysis, we propose novel spectral neural network models based on this representation learning capacity, which exceed current performance benchmarks for multiple temporal knowledge graph datasets.

Within the RPA framework, the 16O nucleus's eigenenergy associated with a dipole resonance is found to be significantly higher in energy than the resonance itself. A similar discrepancy arises when applying the Jost method outside of the RPA framework. We suggest that the RPA's eigenenergy should correspond to the resonance energy even with a potential function that lacks the soliton property. Furthermore, we propose that within the RPA framework, eigenenergies can be categorized into three distinct groups: (1) states closely linked to phonon energy, (2) states unrelated to phonon energy, and (3) states that interact with the phonon in a complicated manner.

Identifying patterns in systems evolving over time through dynamic clustering is a vital aspect of studying time-series data. To enhance the discovery relevant states and structures, it's crucial to refine existing methods for dynamical systems. We introduce a novel algorithm, DBA-Clustering, that determines cluster counts and applies to time-varying systems, finding their significant instances through Impact Based States and applying Time Attention Networks. Our method achieves superior results compared to competitors in benchmark tests and a real-world example involving traffic state clustering.

To overcome under-generated text limitations in Generative Adversarial Network models, we present a sparseGAN variant that incorporates the Generator's input text length into its decision-making process, effectively counteracting under-generation. By integrating the text length as a factor, the author introduces the SparseGAN model, which incorporates the Multi-Head Self-Attention mechanism through Generative Opponent Network to enhance text creation. Experimental results on news article generation demonstrate the superiority of our model over leading baseline models.

The concept of interstellar pansomonia, which suggests that life could be spread across the universe through star-to-star travel, is both alluring and controversial. To explore whether this theory has any credible support, a close examination of existing interstellar pansomonia claims from previous studies has been conducted, focusing on three key criteria: how often interstellar rocks encounter dangerous areas, their ability to protect any life forms they might carry, and the reliability of laboratory findings. Upon detailed analysis, all three candidates were found to have survived unlikely obstacles, another sign that eliminating interstellar transfer barriers is possible.

We have developed a simple model using perturbation and intensity mapping background concepts to predict how disturbances affect HI intensity mapping data that's measured with interferometric instruments. Our model considers how the data is collected, the shape of the observed HI signal, and how these factors interact with the instrument's resolution and detection capabilities. By doing this, we can estimate the hit function, which describes how the data is affected by disturbances on various scales. Our predictions are supported by direct simulations of how the data is measured. When analyzing an infinite plane of mapped regions, our perturbation theory predictions closely match simulations of the data, allowing for accurate assessment of the effect of removing the intensity mapping background. In some cases, up to 20% of the total background can remain after this process. The choice of how to remove the background has significant implications for the accuracy of parameter estimation from hi-res data clusters. We recommend using the Data-driven Background Subtraction (DABS) method, which accounts for the effects of the instrument and the HI signal itself. The effectiveness of this method may be limited by how the data is collected, particularly in experiments that use multiplexed detectors, where the statistical accuracy of this method can be significantly affected, potentially inflating the apparent clustering amplitude by up to 15%. The theoretical predictions made by our model can help guide the selection of experiments and mapping techniques to optimize statistical power and clustering measurements, ultimately pertainting to the validity of cosmological parameter estimation from hi-res data clusters.

We've discovered an unexplored phenomenon, which we call induced spontaneous symmetry disruption chain (ISSDC), while studying topological phases in two-dimensional spin systems beyond the Lindblad equation. Specifically, we've observed that under continuous dissipation, certain topological phases can cause multiple, consecutive breaks of spontaneous symmetry,/spin disordered phases, before reaching a unique ground state. This concept of ISSDC encapsulates the interaction between topological phases and spin disordered phases, and may help us better understand how these elements interplay in quantum many-body systems.

Our new spatial capture-recapture model incorporates an individual's preferred location, integrating field data with economic data on where individuals are most likely to be found. This approach allows us to collect a broader range of recaptured animals by considering their preferred locations in design stratification. The model also helps analyze how external factors, like resource availability, influence movement patterns and population dynamics, while providing location-specific estimates of population size. The framework is demonstrated with real data from tigers in India, and research suggests a two-stage survey design can improve movement model estimates and cost-effectiveness by utilizing data on resource availability.

In networking contexts, estimating minimum energy routes is an essential task.
Given their binary edge costs, finding the lowest energy among $k$ edge-disjoint
$st$-paths that satisfy the connectivity requirement, constitutes a well-known
challenge.  We present an estimation algorithm for this problem, requiring $O(\sqrt{k})$ queries.

This paper puts forward an autonomous method for swarms of unmanned aerial vehicles to break free from both human supervision and reliance on a control center. We propose using arrangements of three-dimensional virtual spaces, or 'supervolumes,' to manage the behavior of the swarm. Each supervolume provides a distinct pattern of flight for the swarm, and they can interact with one another to create more complex routes. A key innovation of our approach lies in its capability to adjust the swarm's supervolumes independently, thus allowing the vehicles to navigate around obstacles without human intervention. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated through computer simulations and a real-world test case, where we successfully guided a swarm of four drones around a stationary object using independently adjusted swarms.

Spatially and temporally varying dynamic processes on activity-based networks display the localization phenomenon, where dynamic phenomena such as quiescent phases and activity bursts occur on activity nodes that are neighboring to one another. Research indicates local interactions drive the emergence of such phases, yet a comprehensive understanding of how networks exhibit this behavior during quiescent and active periods is still lacking. In this research, we employ nodal entropy as an entropy landscape tool to map out quiescent and active regions of dynamic systems on activity-based networks. By applying this approach to both synthetic and real-world data sets, we identify distinct valleys and peaks in entropy space, representing quiescent and active locations respectively. Our results reveal active nodes tend to be centrally located with high centrality measures, while quiescent nodes are more often found at the periphery of the network. Additionally, active nodes usually have more connections than quiescent nodes. Our findings provide an empirical basis for analyzing and comprehending the quiescent and active behavior of dynamic phenomena within network systems.

This research examines defensive effectiveness of teams participating in the 2020 UEFA EURO tournament and 2022 UEFA Nations Cup using statistical methods known as GLM and GLM.

GLM, or the Generalized Linear Model, is used to predict outcomes based on specific characteristics, while its variation, the Generalized Linear Model, encompasses multiple response distributions.

Two specific types of geospatial analysis are performed - point pattern analysis and spatial interaction modeling - to investigate player locations during the events.

Specific techniques including estimating probable future situations and Schoenfeld residuals are also employed in this geographical context.

The results indicate that nations with more experienced squads and those from northern European regions generally excel, and home field advantage provides a significant benefit to participating teams.

Deep Learning techniques have been successfully applied to form extraction and validation, yet they are limited to fixed forms. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a novel approach using visual template matching in a single network, which is the first of its kind. Our model is designed to be device-independent and incorporates text recognition, structural element identification, and logical element identification. It is capable of handling unique and common form elements, as well as implicit design patterns. Our approach achieves remarkable accuracy, outperforming traditional methods in our experiments. We open-source our solution on GitHub under the MIT License.

This work presents a concealed parameter recurrent state space (CP-RSS) framework to modify complex dynamical systems by subtly influencing an observed system's underlying structure. The CP-RSS framework builds upon the concept of latent variables in dynamical systems, introducing a set of hidden variables that represent concealed parameters. By inferring these hidden variables from observed time series data, the CP-RSS framework allows for targeted alterations to specific parameters of the underlying dynamical system. Utilizing a recurrent neural network, this CP-RSS framework predicts the hidden variables and evaluates its performance through numerical experiments with chaotic and periodic dynamical systems. In contrast to previous latent variable models, the CP-RSS framework demonstrates a clearer and more controlled mechanism for modifying the dynamics of complex systems by encapsulating the latent variables within the concealed parameters.

We examine the concept of free conditional independence (FCI) in the context of large random matrices and provide proof that kind $B$ upper triangular matrices, whose entries are conditionally independent given their diagonal entries as independent identically distributed (i.i.d.) variables, exhibit asymptotic kind $B$ freeness. This result has implications for understanding the asymptotic behavior of certain stochastic processes, such as the asymmetric exponential growth process and the Bernoulli-bulk process. We further explore monomial expectations to establish a broader understanding of kind $B$ freeness for matrices associated with the asymmetric exponential growth process and certain random truncations of orthogonal polynomials of the classical type.

We take a type 1 curve C over an algebraically closed field of characteristic 0 and a type 3 cover f: C -> C of type 1. For an odd prime l, we show the Prym variety of f is isomorphic to its Weil pairing dual up to a factor of the form delta, where delta is a subset of Q_(l)^x/(N(K^(l) Q_(l) )Q_(l) ^x), with K being the function field of C and N representing the norm map. Additionally, in a specific scenario, we prove delta equals the trivial set Q_(l)^x/N(K^(l) Q_(l) )Q_(l) ^x, which indicates the intended result for the main conjecture in Iwasawa theory for C.

In the world of evolutionary biology, distinguishing between structural changes and polarization shifts is crucial for pinpointing fundamental polarization patterns within groups of organisms. Although the concept of polarization is universally applicable across various dimensions and dimensions spaces, its vague nature poses a challenge in polarizing complex systems. Particularly in cases where simultaneous structural and polarization changes occur, one major obstacle arises. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach to analyze polarized systems by introducing two distinct types of polarization metrics: those related to orientation and those related to spread. We demonstrate the versatility of this bipartite framework through a case study of bird species, plotting them on a two-dimensional space and discovering two different polarization patterns: a spiral polarization pattern and a fundamental shift in orientation. The proposed method of polarization standardization, which aims to differentiate structural and polarization changes, shows a strong correlation with established standards.

The dynamics of multilayer networks with multiple interaction types are ubiquitous in various systems exhibiting oscillatory behavior. Understanding how to connect the phase oscillator models on separate network layers is crucial in this context. We demonstrate that multilayer networks can exhibit stable, synchronized states where the oscillations propagate through different layers in an isolated manner. For two-layer networks, we derive a fundamental equation that defines a range of parameter values over which these stable states occur. We also identify specific conditions, in the form of matrix inequalities, necessary for the existence of these values. The multilayer network stability can be characterized by a set of multicondensed eigenvalues. We further prove that there is at least one configuration of oscillator frequencies within a range of values, defined by specific inequalities, for which the multicondensed eigenvalues are positive, real, and distinct, for any number of network layers. Additionally, we establish a connection between multilayer network eigenvalues and a set of multilayer tridiagonal matrices, for which we provide an explicit description of their structure, for any number of network layers.

The Cauchy stress function parameterization is commonly utilized in analyzing nonlinear elasticity and computational mechanics due to its convenient formulation of the compatibility and equilibrium conditions, its linearization property under the superposition principle, and its advantage in elemental discretization, where the equilibrium can be enforced at any point within an element. Although Simo and Hughes introduced a related parameterization in 1986, the original form lacked direct physical interpretability. Although a revised version was developed in 2004, its complex expression has hindered its widespread adoption. This research presents a novel, minimal-parameter formulation, which rectifies the limitation of having excessive parameters (4n as opposed to the required 3n) and results in a more straightforward expression, which may facilitate its integration into existing commercial finite elements.

This paper introduces a framework called GP to automate the selection of efficient test cases for evaluating student-generated programs. By employing graph-based metrics, it automatically identifies optimal input cases that effectively validate a program's correctness. Specifically, GP leverages Dependency Spectrum (D-S) and Reachability Spectrum (R-S) to examine all potential input cases, pinpointing the test case with the greatest D-S or R-S value. The application of GP has been demonstrated through the creation of robust test cases for student programs across multiple levels of a coding challenge, namely LeetCode Level 1-3.

Deep learning models, trained on vast datasets of paired words and images, have surprisingly effective results when used to inject domain knowledge into neural networks. Recent studies are now focusing on enhancing the classification of images with contextual cues that guide the focus of analysis. These studies employ large pre-trained models of text-image pairs, which have been trained on millions of datasets, to inject domain knowledge into classifiers that are trained with relatively small datasets. A fundamental question arises whether such models are capable of generalizing across unrelated classes and images, and can they control the distribution of attention guided by textual cues. We introduce HyperPrompt, a novel architecture that addresses these issues, and conduct comprehensive experiments to evaluate hyper-sensitive models to distribution shifts. A key finding reveals that the models' classification of images is typically context-dependent, and most significantly, we observe that HumanTuples pre-trained models, in conjunction with multi-element "hyper-prompts", are exceptionally effective in responding to cues that relate to the class of the target and provide answers that closely resemble human-generated responses.

Let $\sigma$ be a finite vector space over a two-element field, and let $\sigma$ contain the special subgroup $S$. We are examining the longest path that follows an unbroken sequence of distinct representations $\beta$ of $\sigma$, where each subsequent representation is obtained by applying a direct summand of the special subgroup $S$ to the previous one, and no representation lies between them. This is denoted as $\tau(\sigma|S)$. Representations that correspond to an especially complex relationship within the special subgroup $S$ play a crucial role in determining $\tau(\sigma|S)$. As a direct consequence of our research, we can express $\tau(\A_n|\binom{n}{2})$ in a absolute form for any integer $n$ greater than or equal to four.

In quantum optics, both parity and symmetry are widely utilized concepts, yet this work introduces a novel approach linking their effects through super- and bundling operations, specifically exploring parity-symmetry-related phenomena in super-photon bundles. By integrating linear optics with non-linear photon-photon interactions, we demonstrate the ability to achieve super-rapid state changes, both between symmetry groups and parity states, in these bundles. Our study also outlines theoretical conditions for this bundling operation to be effectively reversed, and we derive an equivalent timescale for this process. Interestingly, we find that parity-symmetry-related super-rapid transitions occur most efficiently when using a specific type of unitary evolution, and we explore the concept of "bundling time," offering an equal measure, in this context.

In networks, distance-based metrics are utilized to evaluate structural characteristics. They are particularly valuable in applications where reliability is compromised, such as in the assessment of social networks, which may contain misleading self-reported information. We delve into the fundamentals of network scale estimation, focusing on its statistical underpinnings and practical implementations (including the widely-used "Watts method"). Subsequent to these, we present "WS" and "WS*" methods, which build upon the basics of network scale estimation and employ optimization techniques to minimize the influence of inaccurate data. Our findings indicate that in graphs subject to Byzantine errors (caused by inaccurate or intentionally misleading information), the *WS* method outperforms its counterparts, notably reducing mean squared error in estimation of network parameters.

The success of navigation services relies on accurate short-term traffic estimates, which can be improved without using theoretical traffic models, as shown by recent advances. This approach treats the flow of cars as the flow of particles, and uses this analogy to develop data-driven methods for predicting future queue lengths. By focusing on a single road section, researchers have created a nonparametric technique that can be applied to various road types. The method works by tracking the number of cars ahead of the probe units and those behind, and has been shown to be mathematically sound, providing robust predictions regardless of the units' speed patterns. The effectiveness of this method and its core assumptions were validated through simulations and real-world data, and the results demonstrated high levels of accuracy, with mean absolute relative errors below 15% for both traffic flow and future queue length predictions. Furthermore, the method's flexibility was highlighted, as it allows for seamless adaptation to different scenarios, and has the potential to be integrated with existing traffic estimation models for enhanced performance.

To simulate the dynamics of neutron stars and their subsequent mergers in numerical relativity, neutron star simulations are a crucial component. However, the required boundary conditions for these simulations remain elusive and address a critical gap in data that cannot be circumvented. Constant data, commonly employed as a workaround, often yields unphysical results and fails to accurately reflect conservation laws. In order to develop effective boundary conditions that meet all data needs, both active interfaces and lumped systems demand an real-time data supply that is consistently updated. This paper presents the architecture for a novel, neutron star boundary condition algorithm, which we have named Real-time Neutron Star Boundary, and presents its performance through numerical tests. This algorithm has been coded in C++/SOSevEn and can fulfill all five classes of data requirements, thereby addressing the foundation for successful merger simulations.

The $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ decay channel, though uncommon, can be successfully studied at the LHCb experiment. To increase the available data for this rare decay, the proposed strategy involves selecting $\Sigma^+ $ candidates from $\Lambda _c^+ \to p \Sigma^+ $ decays and removing the $\Lambda $ baryon from the final state of the $\Sigma^+ $ decay. This method effectively enhances the signal significance by an factor of three compared to the standard $\Sigma^+ $ production process.

Recent discoveries of ferromagnetic substances that exhibit superconducting-like Nernst effects near the T-curie point have fundamentally changed the initial assumptions. A ferromagnetic material that displays both giant Nernst effects and suppressed resistivity when combined with itinerant carriers is increasingly appealing for active research. As an exploration, we fabricate both isolated and epitaxial ferromagnetic Mn$_3$NiN films on top of Si$_3$N$_4$ layers, and observe both giant Nernst effects and Hall effects, with the Nernst effect exceeding the T-Curie point by a margin of 3 times. Essentially, the Nernst effect remains prominent, while the Hall effect diminishes beyond the T-Curie point, suggesting possible analogies to the mechanisms present in cuprate superconductors that display massive Nernst peaks.

In the context of autonomous driving systems, learning from instructor-provided video annotations is crucial for developing safety-critical skills. To optimize this process, we present PILE, a novel approach to efficiently distilling knowledge from multiple instructors' data. PILE combines an asynchronous, decentralized training method with lightweight logistic coalition building between model pairs to retain critical information. Our approach minimizes communication with instructors while preserving performance, and outperforms competing methods in zero-shot transfer scenarios, yielding substantial performance gains in scenarios not encountered during training.

This report provides an examination of connections within the category of circular circles, specifically focusing on circular beams and circular reductions. We derive a set of canonical forms for circular beams and the associated matrix for reduced circular entities. A key finding in this research is the capability to simplify reduced circular matrices through one or more modifiable parameters. Notably, we establish the criterion for circular circles to be equivalent to circular reductions. This research was conducted using the framework of Poincar\'e-Lieberman theory.

User centers are crucial for enhancing the resilience of critical services and enhancing their disaster response capabilities. They are evolving from temporary setups to sophisticated facilities packed with electronic devices, compressed air systems, generators, and other machinery that pose safety risks during operations and disposal, particularly in disaster scenarios. This research outlines a comprehensive approach to managing these operations efficiently and securely, leveraging the capabilities of machine learning, particularly in optimizing air consumption for a limited supply of compressed air. The proposed framework is adaptable to various user center configurations and has been successfully implemented at a major scale during Typhoon Hagibis, demonstrating its practicality. Furthermore, this research emphasizes the importance of ensuring the security of these operations and provides a path for future developments in the area.

Laboratory plasmas with varying temperatures often display significant electron and ion temperature differences, and current theoretical models for geodesic acoustic modes (GAMs) do not adequately account for these discrepancies. This work aims to develop a comprehensive theoretical understanding of GAMs by creating a generalized dispersion relation that incorporates both electron and ion temperature parameters. The new dispersion relation is then used to analyze the impact of temperature asymmetries on GAM frequency and amplitude, and to identify the underlying physical mechanisms at play. Furthermore, the relationship between GAM parameters and electron and ion moment equations is established, and the limitations of previously established approximations, such as the long-wavelength and small electron mass assumptions, are explored within the framework of the generalized dispersion relation.

Quantum annealing's search process is significantly hindered by non-stoquastic terms in the annealing Hamiltonian, particularly the leap from a stoquastic Grover mixing Hamiltonian to a non-stoquastic one caused by a transverse field interacting with a thermal bath. Our investigation into the quantum annealing model encompassing this transition reveals that non-stoquastic Hamiltonian terms cause quantum states to oscillate wildly, effectively stunting the annealing process and leading to quadratic performance degradation. Moreover, the model's finding that weak thermal decoherence leads to the absorption of energy and a decrease of quantum states' localization, transforms the annealing process into a disorganized diffusion, causing quantum annealing to fail quadratically faster than its stoquastic counterpart under weak thermal thermal decoherence.

This essay delves into the life and work of Pieter Johannes van Rhijn, an observer who worked under the direction of Kapteyn at the University of Groningen's Kapteyn's Astronomical Institute. Van Rhijn was part of an innovative approach adopted by the institute, which involved delegating specific research tasks to specific experts based on their individual strengths. This approach, implemented by Kapteyn, is explored in detail, along with examples of van Rhijn's work on the brightest stars, which contributed to the institute's renowned catalog projects.

This research paper addresses the following questions: for any specified inertia character and cyclic module of type D, does a corresponding Serre weight exist that is compatible with this Kummer theory? For a positive integer $p\ge3$, let's consider the following conditions: does a strongly irreducible continuous mod $p$ $G_{\Bbb Z_p}$-representation that is not semisimple and has specific reduction properties upon restricting it to $G_{\Bbb Q}_p$ and inertial character exist?

We are studying optimal configurations of n-1 dimensional surfaces in n dimensional space that enclose a specific volume while minimizing their own area, and also have a fixed average curvature. These surfaces often appear as layers within molten materials. We've discovered that many optimal configurations, or 'remnants', of smaller surfaces are embedded within larger ones. A key property of these remnants is their connectivity. To investigate this, we're establishing a mathematical framework to prove the topological equivalence of these remnants. This framework involves analyzing the underlying space and its connectivity through a mathematical measure called 'filling depth'. The scale at which this measure is significant determines the local structure of the surfaces, providing a basis for further study through detailed model calculations. This approach will be demonstrated for several types of surface configurations, such as those modeled after spheres, tori, and minimal surfaces.

The Profound Neural Network (Pronun: PRO-fohnd) demands an enormous number of training parameters and can achieve a strikingly high accuracy of 99.9 percent on 5500 object categories in the ImageNet dataset. Due to its high computational requirements, training the P-NL network on a single processor is both time-consuming and resource-intensive. In an effort to facilitate wider access to the P-NL network, we developed a novel architecture based on two regional evaluator components that train independently using different subsets of data. By utilizing two trainers, we can also distribute the training processors to enhance efficiency. Although there are some limitations in terms of accuracy and field of view, our regional evaluator system exhibits great potential in overall performance. By employing trained processors, we can further optimize the detection of certain object classes, ultimately making the P-NL network more accessible and efficient to use.

A self-sensing composite material that accurately communicates its curvature through harmonic angle is ideal for structure-adaptive electronics. However, factors like material inhomogeneity and manufacturing inconsistencies can distort its harmonic properties. A new method is presented using electrical impedance tomography and optimization to modify the curvature of this material's exact harmonic contour. First, a scan identifies the contour where the material's axial curvature remains consistent. Then, another algorithmic approach transfers this contour to a two-dimensional design, defining points along its length. The results show successful exact transfer of complex, wave-like patterns, including a 25 cm length contour with 2.5 cm period and 0.4 to 0.6 lambda thickness variations.

We propose a novel, user-friendly method for implementing entanglement indicators, specifically designed for complex composite systems. Using this approach, we successfully apply the same indicator to a variety of systems, including Bell's state, Grover's 2-qubit state, superdense coding states, and the three-qubit Greenberger-Horne-Zeyn state, without needing distinct entlement verification methods for each. Moreover, we explore whether entlement verification could potentially occur without direct interaction between the systems' constituent particles.

Mastering repetitive movement tasks through learning from observation and data is often compared to the human ability to quickly acquire new motor skills. Key aspects of this analogy encompass using similar sensors for feedback, applying the same controller to various conditions like different robot sizes or wing shapes, and improving performance by adjusting simple parameters. Through the analysis of highly nonlinear and controllable systems, this work explores simple ways to learn open-loop controls in a model-free setting that meets these criteria. The work's findings are demonstrated to enable swarms of drones to navigate complex environments, build mobile robots to walk steadily, and monarcopters to fly smoothly.

A mathematical framework is presented that utilizes advanced vector and geometric techniques to develop a streamlined method for working with tensors in a Euclidean space. The approach simplifies the tensor representation from rank one to rank three, creating a direct correlation between v-geometric structures and numerical values. This connection facilitates an efficient algorithm for representing three-dimensional objects using symmetric tensors. The proposed method is demonstrated to be a user-friendly and effective system for spatial data analysis. Additionally, a practical application of this framework is provided through the development of a geometric algorithm used to visualize complex data sets, including a visual representation of brain data processed by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). This example utilizes interactive 3D models that can be viewed with basic web technology.

Theoretically, the duration of baseline taste tests should not be constrained by sensor stability. To determine the minimum possible testing duration, we've calculated that it would be achieved with a sensor whose sensitivity fluctuates on a timescale shorter than the testing period. Here, we've explored a scenario where the fluctuation is caused by a new type of light-sensitive particle, resulting in the development of a more efficient taste testing procedure. This procedure minimizes the required number of repetitions per taste and minimizes the sensitivity of the results to the characteristics of this particle, thereby improving testing performance and potentially allowing us to detect a characteristic signature of this particle in the data from the 4Pi taste testing experiment with a small margin of error.

The COVID-19 outbreak forced a sudden transition to a remote learning environment, which significantly impacted the pace and efficiency of students' schedule adherence. To investigate the impact of remote education on students' time management, we collected data via an online survey from both in-person and online learners across the United States. The online sample comprised individuals who learned through remote methods during the COVID-19 pandemic, while the in-person sample consisted of individuals who learned face-to-face. Using descriptive statistics and independent t-tests, our findings indicated that remote learning led to negative consequences on how on schedule learners remained, in contrast to in-person learning outcomes. Furthermore, gender played a crucial role in time management during remote learning processes. To strengthen our online sample's representativeness, we employed stratified random sampling, in line with established research methodologies. Our suggestions include providing in-person learning opportunities during the pandemic to improve schedule adherence and incorporating these findings into broader temporal psychology research.

We have developed comprehensive formulae for applying symmetry principles in $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda field theories at the level of correlations. Specifically, we derive an explicit set of recursive equations for energy levels within dressed states, a key component for understanding the structure of Toda correlations. Building on this, we provide detailed examples of how these energy levels behave in $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ Toda, $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda S-matrix, and form factor frameworks, focusing particularly on two- and three-point arrangements. Additionally, we demonstrate a direct method for obtaining form factors in $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda from scattering data, using it to calculate selected two- and three-point data in the regime where all participants are identical, and verify the results' consistency.
We demonstrate that Coxeter groups possess biautomatic properties, resulting from which we derive that uniform lattices within isometry groups of buildings also exhibit biautomatic structures.

Investigating the thermodynamics and cosmic censorship hypothesis in Reissner-Nordström anti-de Sitter black holes coupled with a scalar field, we found that extremal charge limits in asymptotically flat and anti-de Sitter spacetimes differ, suggesting a modification of the cosmic censorship hypothesis in anti-de Sitter spacetime. Additionally, we examined how thermodynamic phase transitions in this system align with predictions from correspondence principles, revealing complexity in these transitions. A key challenge with these transitions is determining the appropriate critical point locus, which requires incorporating an ensemble of possible thermal states.

In this paper, we adapt the standard ZF axioms to employ four distinct logical systems - classical, paraconsistent, paracomplete, and dialectical logic - in place of the standard classical framework. These revised systems allow for a nuanced analysis of set mathematics, with distinct outcomes for each logical system: in the case of a two-valued system, we recover much of standard ZF set theory; with a three-valued system, we find that most results hold, save for certain size comparisons of specific sets; alternative outcomes emerge when incorporating the dialethis of a four-valued system, with some theorems requiring significant revision; and finally, a dialetheistic system leads to a blend of standard and revised outcomes. We explore the implications of these findings on set mathematics, with a focus on how different logical systems yield diverse results.

Researchers utilized support vector machines to analyze data from an electrocorsugram (ECoG) recording system and determine the ambulatory state of nine human subjects.  The research team designed three different feature sets, with the best performing one consisting of a novel set of coefficients derived from a non-stationary wavelet transform in the time-frequency domain, achieving a classification accuracy of 94.44%.  The study focused on distinguishing between two states of locomotion - stationary walking and free walking - and addressed the challenges posed by the non-stationary nature of brain activity patterns during walking.  Additionally, the research was conducted at a distance of at least 1 meter from the subject, with the ability to differentiate between walking styles at a frequency of 1 Hz.

This paper proposes a new method to calculate entropy and related quantities like mutual information and KL divergence by using nested sampling. Building on this, the researchers demonstrate a connection between entropy and the logarithm of prior factors in this context. Moreover, they provide relevant applications, including parameter estimation, model selection, and inference of unknown functions. To validate their approach, the authors conduct several tests and compare it with other methods, including maximum likelihood, Bayesian inference, and simulation-based methods such as Bayesian parameter estimation, model averaging, and cosmological parameter inference.

We examine how right-angled Artin groups split apart by looking at their representations as fundamental groups of graphs. Specifically, we investigate how these groups divide into smaller parts relative to their index and reveal new ways they can split, taking into consideration their causal patterns on related Cacti complexes. We establish a connection between these dividing patterns and a special type of surface within these Cacti complexes, analogous to a core part of the original group. Through this line of reasoning, we are able to demonstrate that certain complex presentations of these groups by their generators and relations cannot be broken down into simpler presentations by a finite number of elements, particularly when their Causal patterns do not interlock in a specific way.

The brain's dynamic functional connectivity (FC) patterns, which evolve over time, are crucial for understanding neural processing but are computationally expensive to model with current methods. In response, our team developed a novel, efficient approach called Deep Dynamic Efficient Connectivity Estimation (DeepDynEEC), based on a flow-based probabilistic model that captures the complexities of time-series data and indicates a strong correlation with cognitive state changes in the working memory task. Further, we expanded our research to various resting-state and task-based scenarios, discovering that DeepDynEEC's performance significantly surpasses that of top existing baselines across these diverse scenarios, particularly in regions of the brain's prefrontal cortex. Notably, our model's working memory scores also excel when compared to dynamic FC features in regions of the frontal cortex. With its high efficiency, DeepDynEEE can process large-scale data sets, providing a robust solution for analyzing time-varying brain connections on population-level datasets.

The networks we use to represent evolutionary histories are becoming increasingly important across various fields such as ecology, epidemiology, and conservation. As the reliability of these networks is still a topic of discussion, our approach involves expanding on previous research by evaluating how different algorithms construct phylogenetic networks from simulated data with known underlying structures. Through a comprehensive analysis, our study uses simulated datasets encompassing different features such as hybrid nodes and time-scaled information, allowing us to observe the effectiveness of popular methods like APHYON, CHAN, and NNHS in recreating these hybrid networks. Additionally, our results provide a novel perspective by offering an open-source toolkit and emphasizing the significance of selecting an appropriate algorithm considering the specific data characteristics and underlying evolutionary history.

This paper presents a straightforward and straightforward-to-use method for
detecting movement in video footage from living organisms. Our approach is
easy to use and outperforms existing methods, including established techniques-
SVM, Sigmoid, and Threshold. Experimental results show that our method-
called Hinge-outperformsd them. We've made this algorithm accessible through
an open-source implementation using the Python programming language.

High-precision matrix inversion can be achieved through iterative methods such as Neumann series, particularly when the inversion Neumann series is applied to solving linear systems of equations $Ax=b$. This approach can be effective for determining the positions of point sources using interferometry techniques, such as spatial autocorrelation-based methods, which are used in seismic imaging and array processing. However, these methods often require substantial computational time and memory, limiting their capacity for accurately determining multiple source locations, especially in high-resolution seismic surveys or other applications requiring simultaneous inversion of multiple equations. In contrast, a recently proposed method, the Generalized Higher-Order Neumann Series, has been shown to accelerate this process. Building on previous research, a novel technique has been developed that generalizes the GMIB method by incorporating higher-order terms into the Neumann series, allowing the inversion of a single matrix $A$ or multiple matrices $A_i$ for $i=1,2,...,N$ within a Neumann-style formulation, while maintaining the same computational complexity per step, i.e., $O(M^2)$, where $M$ denotes the number of rows in the matrix being inverted. This new approach was experimentally validated and its performance compared to existing methods such as direct inversion, power iteration, and the GMIB method, demonstrating significant improvements in computational efficiency with minimal compromise on accuracy when inverting a single matrix, and substantial accuracy gains of up to 10 times for the inversion of multiple matrices.

In the context of time-varying media, optical devices can efficiently absorb and annihilate incoming waves through a phenomenon known as infinite energy absorption, which occurs at specific frequencies called eigenchannels. The power of these eigenchannels varies across different frequencies, thus affecting their corresponding absorption rates. To examine the energy absorption behavior across a specific range, this paper derives general sum rules for the product of eigenchannel absorption coefficients and their respective powers. The sum rules are formulated based on the scattering parameters of the relevant scattering framework, and concrete applications are explored for the two-channel, symmetric scattering framework with two internal states. The analysis reveals distinct patterns of eigenchannel energy distribution in different regions, with the central region characterized by linear growth of eigenchannel power with frequency, resulting in nearly constant products for eigenchannels with the same symmetry. The two separate sub-frames exhibit cross-talk between internal states, with eigenchannel absorption behaviors largely similar to those in a single isolated frame.

Three-dimensional topological Anderson insulators induced by random disorder are investigated analytically for binary disorder variations. A stochastic Hamiltonian is created to model this system with random perturbations of distinct disorder strengths. A numerical simulation on a finite lattice confirms that the conductance of this system can be controlled by adjusting the probability distribution of these random perturbations. A topological phase transition occurs without a change in the spatial structure of this system, resulting in non-zero conductance. This phenomenon can be observed in the face-centered-cubic lattice topological phase, confirmed numerically. Therefore, this research provides an analytical method to induce topological Anderson conduction in three dimensions with a manageable random disorder distribution.

This paper examines complex multiplicative groups of elliptic curves as complex tori,
exploring how Drinfeld uniformization relates to elliptic curves with complex multiplication.
We provide a comprehensive understanding of isogenies between these trimmed objects,
establishing a connection between Deuring's reduction theorem and the classical Néron mapping
principle for elliptic curves and their endomorphisms over various fields.

The complex parameter space of the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (MSSM) on the Higgs sector calls for a more comprehensive expansion that includes multi-dimensional complex phases and magnitudes of the mu parameter as well as the trilinear and bilinear scalar couplings. This study explores the potential for generating a viable MSSM on-the-shell Higgs sector within this expanded framework, with a specific focus on determining a correct physical value for the lightest CP-even Higgs boson while in a non-degenerate scenario where one scalar is significantly heavier than the other. Furthermore, we examine the implications of this framework on Beyond the Standard Model scenarios, with a particular emphasis on detecting the MSSM Higgs bosons at LHC run 3. Our analysis includes a detailed study of production and decay modes, with a particular focus on diphotons and muon pairs for the lightest Higgs boson. Additionally, we derived and plotted various constraints, with a particular emphasis on the mass and width of the lightest Higgs boson, with a particular focus on the scenario where the mu parameter has a non-zero value of approximately 125 GeV.

A new linearity score has been introduced to effectively distinguish between linear and non-linear transformations in the context of network variations. The linearity score was also used to suggest simple and robust methods for assessing linearity in network transformations, both in supervised and unsupervised scenarios. The effectiveness of the proposed linearity assessment method was verified through simulations and a real-world application. Furthermore, the linearity score was incorporated into a straightforward method for deciding between network autoregressive and non-linear autoregressive models. The theoretical foundations of this method were established, and additional factors were considered to enhance its reliability. The performance of the linearity score and method was confirmed through extensive simulations and the analysis of real data, including results from both simulated and actual datasets. The linearity score method was shown to accurately distinguish between linear and non-linear transformations in network variations, and the proposed method for narar-ninar selection was found to perform well in multiple testing scenarios.

In the realm of optimization, especially in solving complex, high-dimensional problems, declarative techniques like satisfiability-based search have gained significant attention. This approach's advantages extend beyond optimization problems, proving effective in problems with discrete or continuous variables. To facilitate the use of declarative techniques in continuous variable settings, the concept of Deep Declarative Networks (DDNs) was introduced. DDNs integrate optimization frameworks like Support Vector Regression directly into deep learning models to leverage their issue-specific strengths while maintaining learning flexibility through traditional neural network components. This combination's versatility is amplified through subsequent innovations, leading to a comprehensive issue framework that encapsulates an problem's key characteristics. The framework's value is validated through two distinct case studies, examining DDNs' performance with support vector machines and alternative network architectures such as DDNs with ReLU activation, ensuring the study's findings are rigorously tested and the concept's broader applicability confirmed.

A computational, heuristic approach is presented for two biological phenomena: the dispersion of cells through a fluid and the movement of proteins across a lipid membrane. Cell dispersal, a crucial step in development, relies on dispersal forces, including cell-cell adhesion and extracellular matrix interactions. The proposed approach simulates cell behavior, encompassing adhesion, locomotion, and pressure differences across the cell membrane, and is inspired by vertex and level set modeling techniques. The cell dynamics are captured by a single mathematical equation, and a specific method is introduced to modify the cell's surface, followed by a procedure developed for protein distribution. The approach involves multiple steps, including converting the cell surface to a point cloud, applying a level set equation, and using an advecting lipid membrane to simulate protein movement. Two examples are provided to demonstrate the approach's capacity to dispersing cells and protein relocation in response to protein A and protein B interactions.

The NFT and cryptocurrency markets of the blockchain technology rely on settlement,
wherein trading assets and cryptocurrencies are converted into a universally accepted
form of payment, and the nature of this conversion poses a significant security
concern in the context of the cryptocurrency market, especially as it is mostly
based on trust and lacks a rigorous regulatory framework, opening up the possibility
for bad actors to engage in fraudulent activities with a view to confusing the
currency tracer's tracking system and concealing the essence of their illicit
transactions. This research addresses this challenge by exploring various methods
for identifying and uncovering fraudulent activities and presenting a novel approach
for detecting and revealing the currency tracer's trajectory of a suspicious transaction.
To achieve this, we first model the currency tracer's trajectory of a fraudulent
transaction and then propose a new framework for preventing hiding and then uncovering
it. Comprehending Currency Trajectory of a Suspicious Transaction (CCUST) is evaluated
using real-world data with Nintendo tokens, demonstrating its effectiveness in
identifying and revealing the currency tracer's trajectory of a fraudulent transaction
with an accuracy of 99.50%, 99.55%, and 99.45% across different data sets.

Quantum computing's transformative potential in complex computational areas has sparked interest, yet technical challenges, such as quantum noise, hinder practical applications. This study smoothes the path for future quantum computing applications by demonstrating their potential in developing fault-resilient computations. Our research introduces a novel use-case for proximal quantum learning, a new field that combines machine learning and quantum mechanics. Specifically, we integrate reinforcement learning into classical control circuits to optimize quantum computations and counteract quantum errors. By leveraging the collaborative efforts of classical and quantum machines, we overcome the current limitations in reinforcement learning methods. Our results show significant improvements in task success rates and efficiency compared to traditional methods, even when using a reduced number of measurement and processing resources. This achievement highlights the potential of quantum-enhanced reinforcement learning in advancing fault-resilient quantum computation.

Precise timing and frequency measurements typically rely on sensitive resonators with high quality factors.  A novel approach is suggested in this study, using 'double' resonator systems where a critical switch between two states produces a sudden shift in one property, similar to quantum leap metrology.  This method offers an alternative to traditional approaches, avoiding the need for high-quality factors, instead focusing on improved signal-to-noise ratios.  The scheme involves reflecting probes off the coupled resonators and analyzing the change in their reflection coefficients, with the quality factor linked to the change in this coefficient at the transition point.  A particularly effective outcome is achieved in a specific double-cavity setup, resulting in a superior performance that exceeds both classical and quantum limits for precision measurements.

The direct photon-hadron correlation data from the PHENIX experiment have been analyzed for $d+$Au and Au$+$Au collisions at a energy level of 200 GeV. The extracted hadron elliptic flow coefficient, $v_2$, from this data has been compared to 2-particle distribution hadron calculations based on the hydro model with a viscous component, for both types of collisions. Furthermore, the data have been contrasted with the photon-hadron data obtained from $d+p$ collisions at the same energy level, for various photon transverse momentum settings. The findings indicate a reduction in the hadron $v_2$ in $d+$Au collisions when set against Au$+$Au collisions, but this reduction is not as pronounced when comparing it to $d+p$ collisions. A similar trend is observed for photons, where nuclear effects cause a similar reduction in the $v_2$ settings for both hadrons and photons. Additionally, the magnitude of this reduction is found to be similar for both hadrons and photons at each photon transverse momentum configuration.

The Smarandache's sigma digit multiplication sequence is an exploration of the time it takes for the product of a number and integers starting from 1, to have a sum of digits that matches the initial number, identifying the smallest number that fulfills this criteria for each multiplication.

Large-scale simulations of complex physical phenomena are frequently carried out as an overlay network, often referred to as "Sound," over the underlying Internet infrastructure. These simulations demand high bandwidth and low latency for effective performance, which can be achieved by increasing the size of the simulation domain through parallel processing. However, processing gains are undermined by inter-processor communication overhead as the number of processors grows, leading to a decrease in network efficiency and eventual limitation on scalability.

This research深入 analyzes the relationship between network efficiency and the effective bandwidth available per processor in the Sound network, which has significant implications for scalability. It shows that due to variability in network efficiency, it's difficult to forecast how a Sound application will scale based solely on increasing the number of processors and maintaining the same level of efficiency. Moreover, the study reveals that the impact of efficiency fluctuations on application performance is more severe at lower levels of efficiency and lower in the high-efficiency range. As a result, it's observed that while it's possible to scale up the number of processors used without affecting the application's efficiency by decreasing the load on each processor, there's a corresponding decrease in the effective bandwidth available per processor, leading to potential limitations on the scalability of the application.

We investigate a new online learning scenario called distributed situational linear bandits, where a team of decision-makers learns from their individual experiences to improve, without exchanging their past data. This happens across different environments, or situations, and the decision-makers' challenges are connected through a common pattern of information. We establish connections between this new scenario and existing pattern-based learning models and show how a new simple algorithm can ensure the team grows at nearly the best possible rate, leveraging their shared information. This algorithm delivers optimal results for several well-known pattern types, including when the part of the decision-makers' challenge that's consistent is large, when it's the random elements that's constant, and even when the decision-makers' challenges are opposed.

Over the past decade, working from home has become increasingly prevalent globally. Despite its benefits in reducing travel costs and enhancing work-life balance, its impact on agile project success remains unclear. To explore the dynamics of remote working in relation to scrum project success, this research combines theoretical models and practical data through an PLS-SEM analysis and a neural network method called SmartPLS 3 and an artificial neural network. It involves 133 professionals working from home on scrum projects and highlights the importance of several factors including self-discipline, self-efficacy, and available technology. The study's findings provide valuable insights for organizations looking to implement remote working arrangements for their scrum projects.

Our study employs traditional formalisms in event shape engineering to examine how the elliptic motion, represented by v2, responds to in-plane and out-of-plane direction in lead-lead collisions at 2.76 TeV. By utilising charged-particle flow coefficients measured over a central rapidity interval to control these motions, we found that the v2 to v3 ratio exhibits a characteristic sine wave pattern in pp and p-p collisions, but this is altered due to initial geometry in Pb-Pb collisions. Additionally, the v2 to v3 ratio reveals an important insight into the interplay between the interplay of interplay of two v2 components, and how they affect each other, providing valuable information about the viscous nature of the quark-gluon plasma created in these collisions.

This paper introduces the Quaternion Linear Canonical Stockwell Transform and derives formulas for its inverse, along with kernel space characterization, to facilitate its inverse reconstruction. We also establish the ambiguity and joint ambiguity theorem for this transform.

The extremal GDoF advantage of employing an optimal power regulation scheme over a binary power regulation scheme in a K-user interference network is $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$ times greater. Notably, the benefit of optimal power regulation in a K-user interference network is directly proportional to $\sqrt{K}$, which also indicates its $\Theta(K^{0.75})$ relationship with a multi-access $K$-user network. Furthermore, our vector coding approach achieves the highest possible GDoF advantage for both type power regulation schemes in binary regulated scenarios.

A novel multi-time-step integration technique has been developed for use in particle simulations, where forces are applied at disparate time intervals. Instead of adopting a traditional assumption of instantaneous particle collisions, this technique better reflects the reality of finite-duration collisions. The method treats collisions over a defined period, during which integrator steps are applied. In this framework, an analytical solution is established at the conclusion of the collision duration and influences the method's consistency. This approach can be viewed as incorporating a gradual transition phase between discrete time intervals. We demonstrate that this technique provides a flexible framework that aligns with experimental data from previous studies. However, it also poses challenges due to the complexity of numerical calculations. To overcome this, a targeted formulation has been developed to facilitate particle simulations. In this context, several characteristics are crucial for achieving desirable results. Notably, this technique has been shown to yield satisfactory outcomes when applied to simulations of turbulent flows containing particles. We demonstrate that this technique is feasible when combined with existing numerical computation techniques, notably the finite-volume method. Notably, this technique has been applied to several particle simulations of finite, infinite, and finite geometries. Notably, this technique has been shown to produce results comparable to those of traditionally used techniques, notably the heuristic impulse-based method. Notably, this technique has been shown to facilitate more realistic particle collisions by accounting for the effects of particle spin and deformation.
